newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian lev seen sliding despite high rates.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian lev seen sliding despite high rates.

text.p: Bulgaria should seek ways other than high interest rates to support the lev, pressured by a stagnating economy, expectations of soaring inflation and bank instability, a leading local financier said on Wednesday.
"The high interest rate can no longer support the lev, it only stifles the market," manager of Adlon Discont financial house Andrei Pramov told Reuters.
"The restrictive policy of the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) has exhausted its potential," he added.
The BNB has raised the central interest rate four times this year to a record 108 percent, in force since May 10, when the lev hit a historic low of 150 to the dollar.
The rate rise, accompanied by draconian restrictive measures, helped steady the lev for a week at around 108 to the dollar. Since then it has slid gradually to a record low today of around 203.

Central Bank governor Lyubomir Filipov said recently that the rate could not be reduced until monthly consumer price inflation was curbed to a single-digit figure. Consumer inflation rose in August to 23.3 percent from 20.3 in June.
"It is impossible to rely solely on a high central interest rate for restoring confidence in the national currency and the banking system," said Pramov, a former chief dealer with Economic Bank.
A lower central interest rate would give the economy more breathing room, he said.
The BNB's foreign exchange trade regulations can, if enforced properly, provide adequate controls against speculative forex trade and support the lev, said Pramov.
In an ambitious reform programme sealed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) last month the BNB pledged to cut completely uncollateralised lending to commercial banks.
Bulgaria also pledged to curb monthly inflation to 2.5 percent by year-end. The National Statistics Institute predicts 1996 inflation will be 150 percent.
Three months ago the central bank sought to have five major banks declared bankrupt in a bid to offset a grave bank crisis, though the courts will not rule on this until September.
High interest rates will cause more banks to fail as they have difficulty covering interest payments and have chronic liquidity problems resulting from BNB restrictive measures.
"With looming bankruptcies, soaring inflation and stagnant production one cannot expect rising confidence in either the lev or in the banks," said Pramov.
The lev should gradually fall to its real value against the dollar by shedding one lev of its value each day, said Pramov.
The current exchange rate does not compensate for the vast gap between interest on dollar deposits of four percent and interest on lev deposits of 108 percent, he added.

High rates have also shrunk the local interbank forex market to half a dozen participants. All big dollar clients are now being serviced by local branches of foreign banks like Raiffeisenbank Bulgaria AD and ING Bank, said Pramov quoting BNB forex trade reports.
Lower interest rates would also relieve some of the burden on the budget deficit as maturity payments now exceed net sales of government securities.

Bulgaria's finance ministry will place 20 billion levs worth of treasury bills in three auctions on Friday and Monday. Dealers predict a total of around seven billion levs of T-bills will be subscribed in the three issues.
"There is no adequate supply of goods and services to absorb the ever increasing money supply produced by the current macroeconomic policy," said Pramov.
Battling a serious economic crisis triggered by delayed reforms, the government agreed with the IMF to close down scores of loss-making enterprises, but has been slow to start doing so.
-- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
